lines: Cracked handles are small <shake>warnings</shake> with expensive timing.
A dull edge makes every simple job into a bad plan.
A handle should fit the hand, not argue with it.
A sharp edge is useful. A careless one is just trouble with shine.
The bench hears every complaint before the finished tool gets praised.
Cracked handles are warnings. Ignore them and they become stories.
Most days, I am at the smithing table, trying to keep edges and handles from becoming everyone else's problem.
People think tools is simple until something goes wrong and suddenly it is very important.
A village runs on small work. Nobody praises it until it stops happening.
I trust a good file more than a loud promise. The file has less to prove.
That time I followed you, the whole plan could have used a better handle.
I remember following you through that road. My feet remember it even better.
That trip across that road taught me to ask more questions before walking.
Following you taught me that plans sound much safer before anyone starts walking.
I kept up, mostly. My feet have a harsher opinion of the trip.
Next time, warn me before the road becomes a test of character.
I learned two things out there: stay close, and ask better questions earlier.
You move like danger is a normal part of the route. I am still adjusting to that.
It was not all bad. Some views are worth sore legs and nervous glances.
If I followed you again, I would pack more food and fewer assumptions.
A boat is just a tool with a nervous floor. Yours worked, mostly.
That boat trip still sits oddly in my memory, but at least it floated.
A boat can make a bad plan quieter. It can't make me forget it.

I notice the little things. That is either a skill or what the smithing table has done to me.
